book: 047 - Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

chapters.relation: Argues that shonen fighting anime stage a choice between Adam Smith's and Darwin's models of competition: Zoro hunting Mihawk in One Piece, Goku's technique-by-technique training, and Rock Lee's specialization show competition improving people within the limits of a human excellence, while Cell's absorbing evolutions, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's risky hollowification represent limitless 'leveling up' that changes what you are. The chapter concludes that the Darwinian win-at-all-costs model produces the perpetually dissatisfied Vegeta, and that framing competition around being a certain kind of person (a great swordsman, not just a winner) gives life a completable aim — while conceding that Darwinians rightly warn our picture of the 'normal human' has unjustly cast off jinchūriki like Naruto and Gaara and Devil Fruit users like Luffy.

Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.

Argues Astro Boy re-enacts the sacrificial logic of the atomic age: Atomu is the nuclear-powered copy of the dead Tobio, born from Dr. Tenma's refusal to accept mortality, and his repeated self-sacrifice for humans who discard him (as in 'Save the Classmate,' where the rescued boys' parents still want him removed) shows him functioning as Heidegger's 'standing-reserve' — an object valued only as stored power, with humans themselves next in line. Drawing on Plato's Republic anxiety over originals and copies, Adorno and Horkheimer's dialectic of enlightenment, and Rey Chow's account of mimesis as the sign left by sacrifice, the chapter reads the series as mourning an innocence that became impossible after Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Argues that Grave of the Fireflies works as a critique of anime's child-hero convention: Seita acts exactly like a plucky anime protagonist when he defies his not-actually-evil aunt, strikes out on his own with Setsuko, ignores the farmer's advice to apologize and return, and demands a quick fix from the doctor — but these 'heroic' choices kill them both, because he lacks the developed capacity to reason. Against the medieval 'child as little adult' picture that most anime (Dragon Ball, Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!) romanticizes, the chapter deploys Aristotle's view of children as unfinished beings who cannot yet reason or achieve happiness, concluding the film is a cautionary tale about the years of nurture and guidance real children need.

Reads alchemy's law of equivalent exchange as a parable of capitalism: Locke's labor-mixing argument explains how hours of a life become property and why money is 'distilled life'; Aristotle's attack on limitless wealth-getting (the Midas problem) and Aquinas's capital vices explain how pursuing money for its own sake brings the homunculi — Greed, Pride, and the Sloth the Elric brothers' forbidden act produced — into the world. Marx's 1844 Manuscripts supply the punchline that money performs 'human alchemy' on people, buying their time, esteem, and bodies the way red stones are made from sacrificed humans, so the chapter concludes that capital, like the Philosopher's Stone, profits only by consuming lives and that markets must be held to a promise of fairness and care beyond mere exchange.

Traces hentai from Hokusai's 'Diver and Two Octopi' through the 1920s eroguro journals to the Lolita Anime and Cream Lemon OVAs, then asks whether even this extreme material has value as fantasy. The chapter frames the media-effects debate with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis (revived by Feshbach and tentatively supported by Milton Diamond's finding that Japanese rape rates fell as pornography spread) against Plato's Republic worry that sensational works license irrationality (updated by the Disinhibition, Desensitization, and Cultivation theories), and concludes that hentai's real harm is attitudinal rather than behavioral: its ritual 'breaking' of strong women and sex-as-something-done-to-passive-girls cultivates misogyny and a dehumanizing view of sex.

chapters.file: ch30 - 18 - The Devil Within Sara Livingston.md
ch32 - Who Wants to Be Human Anyway.md
chapters.relation: Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.

Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.

chapters.file: ch34 - One Last Anguished Existential Scream.md
chapters.relation: Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.

A closing personal essay arguing that anime's defining gift is the genuinely unexpected — a robot sprouting from Naota's forehead bump in Fooly Cooly, Berserk's catastrophic finale, Samurai Champloo's Edo-meets-hip-hop fusion, Paprika's dream parade — which jolts viewers into noticing and rethinking their expectations, the very opening that philosophic inquiry requires. It also credits anime's sincere, two-way engagement with its audience (the cast-and-crew interviews on DVD extras that won the author over) for the genre's ongoing, unpredictable evolution.

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection models competition as open-ended selection with no fixed notion of the 'best' form of life.
holes.why: Chapter 22 structures its entire argument as Adam Smith's limited, humanity-bounded competition versus Darwin's unlimited evolutionary 'leveling up,' using Cell, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's hollowification as Darwinian cases.

holes.name: Mimesis (art as imitation of life)
holes.what: The ancient concept of representation as imitation, whose Platonic critique (copies at removes from truth) and modern sacrificial reading (Rey Chow) treat the copy as bearing the marks of what it replaces.
holes.why: Chapter 25's central analytic tool is mimesis: Atomu is a robot copy of the dead Tobio whose imperfect imitation of the human both channels and exposes the violence of the atomic age, and no existing slug covers imitation-in-art.

holes.name: Catharsis (purging of emotion through art)
holes.what: Aristotle's Poetics idea that sensational art cleanses spectators of pent-up emotions, safe-keeping them from acting those feelings out; the modern 'catharsis theory' of media violence descends from it.
holes.why: Chapter 29's core debate is whether hentai purges or feeds violent desire, staged explicitly as Aristotle's catharsis versus Plato's Republic alarm, with Feshbach, Berkowitz, and cultivation theory as modern heirs.

holes.name: Arthur Koestler
holes.what: Essayist whose The Ghost in the Machine (1967) treats consciousness as emergent, pictures minds as 'holons' that preserve individuality within evolving wholes, and links self-transcendence to Eastern mysticism.
holes.why: Chapters 32 and 33 are built on Koestler: the manga's title comes from his book, the Major's merger with the Puppet Master illustrates his holon theory, and Oshii's Innocence is read as deliberately subverting him.

holes.name: Donna Haraway
holes.what: Feminist theorist of the cyborg whose 'A Cyborg Manifesto' treats the human–machine hybrid as breaking gender dualisms and rejecting both biological essentialism and goddess-nature feminism.
holes.why: Chapter 33 reads Major Kusanagi as Haraway's post-gender cyborg enacted, quotes the Manifesto throughout, and names the film's forensic scientist after her; no taxonomy slug covers her.

holes.name: Transhumanism and the Singularity
holes.what: The view that technology can and should carry human beings beyond biological limits, culminating in a Singularity where superhuman, self-evolving intelligence supersedes our species.
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues the net-born Puppet Master dramatizes the Singularity (via Vinge and Kurzweil) and reads the film's ending as transhumanist techno-transcendence, a frame taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Anxiety (Angst)
holes.what: Heidegger's objectless state-of-mind in Being and Time in which the world feels unhomelike and the everydayness of 'the They' collapses, opening the choice of authentic existence.
holes.why: Chapter 34 explicitly develops Heidegger's Being-and-Time account of anxiety (not Kierkegaard's) to explain Shinji's screams and SEELE's leap into the Human Instrumentality Project.
